sec: Phosphate wasting, inherited rickets and replacement

items.q: Match the following hypophosphatemic-rickets inheritance patterns — 1) X-linked 2) Autosomal recessive 3) Autosomal dominant … A) DMP1 B) PHEX C) FGF23
items.exp: The source lists PHEX for the common X-linked form, DMP (DMP1) for a recessive form and FGF23 for the dominant form. (Book p891)

items.q: A family has phosphate-wasting rickets with an X-linked pattern. Which gene is the best match to the chapter's commonest inherited form?
items.exp: PHEX-related disease is the most common inherited hypophosphatemic rickets form named in the table. (Book p891)

items.q: An FGF23 variant resists proteolytic cleavage. Which combination of intact FGF23 action and serum phosphate is expected?
items.exp: The later laboratory note correctly links phosphate wasting to increased FGF23 activity. The table's downward arrow should be treated as an error, and PHEX/DMP1 regulation is more complex than direct cleavage alone. (Book p891)

items.q: Match the following typical rickets laboratory findings — 1) Serum phosphate 2) ALP 3) Calcium and PTH … A) Raised B) Usually normal C) Low
items.exp: The page lists low phosphate, increased ALP and normal calcium/PTH in inherited hypophosphatemic rickets. (Book p891)

items.q: A child has lower-limb deformity, low phosphate, high ALP and normal calcium and PTH. Which disorder best fits?
items.exp: Lower-limb-predominant rickets with isolated phosphate wasting matches the source phenotype, rather than a primary calcium/PTH disorder. (Book p891)

items.q: Which is the odd one out among causes of renal phosphate wasting on this page?
items.exp: The renal causes include proximal tubular dysfunction/type II RTA, inherited rickets and tubular injury; loss of FGF23 action promotes phosphate retention. (Book p891)

items.q: An adult develops bone pain, weakness and phosphate wasting from a mesenchymal tumor. What is the best mechanistic explanation?
opts: Suppressed proximal phosphate transport from absent PTH
items.exp: Tumor-induced osteomalacia is typically due to FGF23 secretion by a mesenchymal tumor. The source's 'gain-of-function mutation' shorthand should not imply that such a mutation is required in every case. (Book p891)

items.q: The source's daily phosphorus requirement entry is ___, while each listed Adphos tablet is ___.
items.exp: The page prints a 2 g daily requirement and 250 mg Adphos tablets; the requirement is a source-specific teaching value, not a universal dietary recommendation. (Book p891)

items.q: Using the page's low-fat-milk phosphate concentration of 0.9 mg/mL, 250 mL provides approximately ___ mg.
items.exp: 0.9 × 250 = 225 mg. Low-fat milk is listed as an oral source for mild depletion. (Book p891)

items.q: Match the following replacement entries — 1) Mild depletion 2) Severe depletion 3) Dietary source … A) IV phosphorus B) Oral phosphate tablets C) Low-fat milk
items.exp: The chapter separates oral replacement for mild disease from IV replacement for severe disease and also lists low-fat milk. (Book p891)

items.q: Which IV phosphorus regimen is printed for severe hypophosphatemia?
items.exp: The source gives 10 mg/kg over 12 hours. Actual IV phosphate prescribing requires a validated preparation-specific protocol, renal assessment and calcium/phosphate monitoring. (Book p891)

items.q: Compare the mild-phosphate entries: I The opening diagram labels asymptomatic 1–2.5 mg/dL as not needing treatment. II The final page discusses oral replacement for mild disease.
items.exp: Both statements occur in the source. They should not be collapsed into a universal treat-all or treat-none rule. (Book p891)
